title: Why start here
paras: Why start here? Because almost every expensive mistake in planning traces back to starting in the wrong place. People reach for the policy, the design, the neighbours — before settling the three questions that come first, and those decide everything after. So we take them in strict order. One thing up front: I'm keeping the section numbers, case citations and exact statutory wording out of this — they all live in the written guide.

The three are these. First — is what you're proposing development at all? If it isn't, the planning system has nothing to say. Second — if it is, where does permission come from? There are only two possible sources, and which one applies changes everything you do next. Third — once permission exists, has development lawfully begun? A permission that's never lawfully implemented is worth nothing, and a lot of value gets destroyed every year by people who thought they'd started when they hadn't.

The order matters because each question leans on the one before. You can't ask where permission comes from until you know you need it, or whether development's begun until there's a valid permission to begin. Take them out of sequence and you've built the analysis on air. It's dull, unglamorous — and the single most valuable habit in the field.

title: The starting point: section 55
paras: The starting point is one word: development. It has two limbs, joined by 'or'. The first is operations — building, engineering, mining or other operations, on or under the land: the digging, building, altering of the land itself. The second is a material change in the use of buildings or land — not physical works, but what the land is used for and whether that's changed in a way that matters. 'Material' just means significant enough to count in planning terms, as opposed to trivial.

Put that with the gateway rule and you've got the founding principle: permission is required for development, and only for development. If what you're proposing doesn't fall within the definition, it isn't development, the requirement isn't engaged, and planning control has nothing to say. That's why the first question is never 'will I get permission' — it's 'do I need permission at all'.

title: The first limb: operational development
paras: Take the limbs in turn, starting with operational development — building, engineering, mining or other operations. The Act helps on building operations: it includes demolition, rebuilding, structural alterations or additions, and — an open phrase — other operations normally done by someone in business as a builder. If it's the kind of thing a builder does, it's likely a building operation. Engineering operations is what an engineer would do — reprofiling land, forming accesses and hardstandings, ponds, bunds, earthworks. Mining is the winning of minerals. And 'other operations' is the catch-all, though the courts keep it tied to a physical operation on the land.

The recurring question is: when is a structure actually a building? Because if it is, putting it up is operational development that needs permission; if it isn't, it may escape the definition. This is a matter of fact and degree — no bright line, you weigh the facts. Three factors do most of the work: size — is it substantial? Permanence — there for a limited period, or indefinitely? And attachment — fixed to the ground, or just resting on it? Large, permanent, fixed is a building; small, temporary, free-standing usually isn't.

The other side of that coin is the chattel — a movable object that isn't part of the land, something you could pick up and take away. A garden bench, a portable cabin, a shipping container dropped on the ground: all can be chattels rather than buildings, on those same three factors. The classic borderline is the caravan, and mobile structures generally — decades of argument, and their own study with their own statutory tests of what counts and how many go where.

One more feature, and it matters later: operations happen at a moment, uses continue. An operation is a completed act — dig the trench, pour the concrete, raise the wall, and at some moment it's done. A use carries on over time. That difference runs right through the system, and it's why the enforcement time limits treat operations and uses differently.

title: The second limb: material change of use
paras: The second limb — material change of use — is subtler, and it's where the real judgement lives. A change of use can be development even where not a brick moves. The question is whether the use has changed, and whether that change is material — significant in planning terms, rather than trivial — judged as fact and degree. The test isn't whether the owner's done something different; it's whether the change matters for the use and development of land.

Start with the planning unit — you can't judge whether a use has changed without deciding what area of land you're looking at, the parcel considered as a whole. Too large — taking in land that functions separately — and a big change on one part gets lost in the whole. Too small — carving out a corner that's really part of a bigger whole — and an ordinary incident of the main use looks brand new. The normal starting point is the unit of occupation: the area in one person's control, used for one main purpose. But where genuinely separate activities go on in physically distinct parts, each can be its own unit.

Then primary and ancillary uses. Within a unit there's usually one primary use — the main thing the land's for — and maybe one or more ancillary ones that serve it: the office in a factory, the store in a shop. An ancillary use needs no permission of its own; it's part and parcel of the primary use. The danger is the ancillary use that grows — storage ancillary to a shop until the storage is the real business, a hobby in a garage that becomes commercial vehicle repair. At some point of fact and degree it stops serving the main use and becomes primary in its own right — a material change needing permission, even though nothing was ever formally 'started'.

A few more: intensification, mixed uses and houses. Intensification — much more of the same thing — can be a material change if it's great enough to change the character of the use in planning terms; though the courts are cautious, and a mere increase in activity isn't automatically development. A mixed use — two or more uses running together, neither merely ancillary to the other — is itself a distinct use, so moving to a mixed use, or altering the balance of one, can be material. And housing: turning a single dwelling into a house in multiple occupation, where unrelated people share facilities, may or may not be a material change — it depends on the scale, character and size of the house.

There's one change the Act puts beyond argument: using a building previously a single dwelling as two or more separate dwellings is always a material change — of the building, and of each part so used. It doesn't matter how small the works, or whether there are any at all. Splitting one house into separate homes is development, full stop, and it always needs permission unless permission comes from somewhere automatic.

title: What is not development: section 55(2)
paras: Now for what's not development. Having defined it broadly, the Act carves out a list of things declared not to be development. Four are worth pulling out.

First, internal and non-external works. Maintenance, improvement or alteration that affects only the interior, or doesn't materially affect the external appearance, isn't development — you can remodel the inside freely, as far as planning's concerned. Building regulations, and for listed buildings listed building consent, are another matter; it's the external effect that engages planning control. Second, incidental uses within the curtilage of a house — the garden and yard that go with it. Using them for a purpose incidental to enjoying the house isn't development: the greenhouse, storing the car, a home gym. But it doesn't stretch to a full commercial business — run a haulage yard from the back garden and you're outside the exclusion, into a material change of use.

Third, agriculture and forestry — the one most often misread. The use of land for agriculture or forestry, and the use of a building occupied with it for those purposes, isn't development. It's the use that's excluded, not the building work. Putting up an agricultural building is an operation — operational development — which may be permitted development under the Order, but it isn't taken outside the definition here. The farmer erecting a large barn is carrying out development; only the agricultural use of the land is declared not to be. Fourth, changes within the same use class: where a use falls within one of the classes in the Use Classes Order, changing to another use within the same class isn't development — and that works hand in glove with the Order that grants permission for certain changes between classes.
So the broad definition isn't the last word. A competent analysis checks the exclusions before concluding permission is needed at all.

title: The cascade
paras: And so to the cascade — the spine that holds all of this together. Faced with any proposal, take three steps, in order, and don't move on until the current one's answered.

Step one: is it development? Apply the definition — an operation, or a material change of use — and does any exclusion take it out? If not, stop; control isn't engaged. Step two: if it is, does the permitted development order already grant permission for it? Only two sources — an automatic grant by that Order, or an express grant on an application. Look to the Order first, because if it's permitted development, permission already exists and no application's required. Step three: if the Order doesn't grant it, an express application is required. There's no third way.

And it's astonishing how often the cascade gets ignored. People argue the merits of a scheme before establishing it's development; assume an application's needed without checking the Order; or assume the Order covers them without checking it's development at all. Taking the three in sequence, every time, is the most valuable working habit in planning. Not clever — just disciplined.

title: Permitted development is planning permission
paras: This one deserves its own section, because so many people — some who should know better — get it wrong. The belief is that permitted development doesn't need planning permission. It's false, and understanding why unlocks the whole thing. All development needs permission, without exception. What the permitted development order does is grant that permission in advance, automatically, for the classes it describes. So permitted development isn't development that escapes the need for permission — it's development for which permission has already been granted, by the Order rather than the council. The permission is real.

Three consequences follow. First, the limitations define the grant. Each class grants permission up to defined limits — dimensions, distances, positions, volumes, various exclusions. Those aren't policy to be weighed; they're the boundary of the grant itself. Exceed one, by any margin, and the grant doesn't apply — and there's no permission for the whole development, not just for the excess. A rear extension half a metre too long isn't mostly permitted with a small overhang to sort out; it's an extension the Order gives no permission for at all, wholly unauthorised unless you apply.

Second, conditions attach. Because it's a permission, it can carry conditions, and many classes do. Some are simple — materials must match. Others require prior approval. Prior approval is a condition of a permission that already exists: before development begins, the developer asks the authority to approve certain specified matters, and only those. The authority isn't deciding whether to grant permission — that's already granted — it's policing a closed list, transport, contamination, flooding, design, depending on the class, and it can't refuse on anything outside it. And in many classes, if the authority doesn't determine the request within the statutory period, approval is deemed given by default and the developer can proceed.

Third, the automatic grant can be taken away. An Article 4 direction, made by the local authority, withdraws permitted development rights for particular development in a particular area — commonly a conservation area, or somewhere under development pressure. It doesn't make the development unlawful in principle; it removes the automatic grant, so what would have been permitted now needs an express application in the ordinary way. It returns the development to the application route — it doesn't forbid it.

title: The trap inside article 3: habitats
paras: Now a trap sitting inside the grant, missed even by professionals because it lives in a different piece of legislation — the habitats regulations. The grant of permitted development isn't unconditional; it's made subject to those regulations, which bite where otherwise-permitted development is likely to have a significant effect on a European site — the top-tier protected habitats, the Special Areas of Conservation and Special Protection Areas that carry the highest level of nature protection.

Where that risk exists, the development must not begin until the developer has applied to the local authority and got its written approval — and that can only be given after the authority has carried out an appropriate assessment, a formal assessment of the effect on the site, in consultation with Natural England. Until then the Order's grant is switched off, and development begun without it is unauthorised, exactly as if the Order had never applied.

Why it matters so much is the overlap. The development that leans hardest on permitted development rights — agricultural buildings, barn conversions to housing, rural changes of use — tends to happen in exactly the rural areas where European sites and their catchments are. A farmer on an agricultural class, or a landowner converting a barn, can be within the Order's limits and still be caught, and neither the Order nor the ordinary guidance shouts about it. So anyone advising near a protected site, or in a nutrient-sensitive catchment, checks the habitats position before telling a client to crack on — because 'it's permitted development, go ahead' is worthless if the regulations have quietly withdrawn the grant.

title: Knowing for certain: lawful development certificates
paras: So how do you know for certain? If permitted development is a permission you can't see — because no council ever issued a decision notice — how do you prove you've got it? And how do you prove an existing use or building has become lawful with time? The answer is the lawful development certificate, and it works in two directions.

One is forward-looking: you ask the authority to certify that a proposed use or operation would be lawful if carried out — because it's permitted development, or isn't development at all. Certainty before you act. The other is backward-looking: you ask them to certify that an existing use, existing operations, or something done in breach of a condition, is lawful now — because it's permitted development, or the time for enforcement has passed.

Three things to fix in mind. The test is legal, not planning merit — not whether the thing is acceptable or well designed, only whether it's lawful. A hideous but lawful thing gets a certificate; a beautiful but unlawful one doesn't. The burden's on the applicant, on the balance of probabilities — more likely than not that the facts and the law support lawfulness. And certificates are won and lost on evidence. Contemporaneous documents — dated invoices, photographs, utility bills, tenancy agreements, statutory declarations — carry far more weight than a recollection offered years later. So build the evidence base as you go, not when the dispute arrives.

title: Commencement: section 56
paras: Now the third foundational question, forgotten until it's too late: has development lawfully begun? A permission doesn't last forever. The standard one must be begun within three years of being granted — some carry a different period, but three years is the norm — and if it isn't lawfully begun in time, it lapses. A lapsed permission is dead: the value it represented, sometimes very large, is gone, recoverable only by applying again in a policy world that may have moved against you.

Development is taken to begin on the earliest date any material operation in it starts to be carried out. The material operations are a defined list: construction work erecting a building; demolition; digging a trench for the foundations; laying an underground main or pipe to those foundations or that trench; laying out or constructing a road; and a change of use amounting to material development. The list is generous. A modest but genuine start — digging a foundation trench, forming part of the access — is enough in law to implement a permission and keep it alive indefinitely after. That's technical commencement, nothing improper: a developer not ready to build out in full, but who doesn't want to lose the permission, can carry out a real material operation to preserve it. The key words are real and genuine — a token gesture, or a sham, won't do.

And here's the trap — the Whitley principle, which destroys permissions every year. It isn't enough that your works are on the list; they must also be lawful, carried out in accordance with the permission and its conditions. Many permissions carry pre-commencement conditions — conditions precedent that must be satisfied before any development begins. Carry out your material operation before discharging one, and your works are in breach — and works in breach of a condition aren't carried out under the permission, so they commence nothing. The clock runs, the three years expire, the permission lapses, even though the developer thought they'd started. The courts have softened it at the edges, and there are cases where a breach isn't fatal — but those are lifeboats, not a route.

So the practical rule, and treat it as absolute: before any material operation to implement a permission, do three things. Discharge every pre-commencement condition first. Get the authority's approvals in writing. And record the implementing works with dated photographs, so if it's ever disputed you can prove what you did and when.

Two consequences after commencement. There's no going back — once lawfully begun, a permission can't be abandoned; there's no doctrine by which a landowner just gives one up. It runs with the land and endures. And the levy — commencement is the moment Community Infrastructure Levy liability crystallises, where the levy applies. Any reliefs or exemptions, and there are valuable ones, have to be claimed and formally confirmed before development begins, and in most cases a commencement notice served first. Start on site before the paperwork's in order and the relief is lost irretrievably — the levy becomes payable in full, often as a surcharge, no way back.

title: Common misconceptions
paras: Now the confident errors that recur so often they're worth naming. First: 'permitted development doesn't need permission.' It is permission, granted in advance by the Order — exceed a limitation and the grant fails entirely, and the whole development's unauthorised. Second: 'it's only temporary, so it's fine.' Temporariness isn't an exemption — a change of use, or an operation, can be development whether or not it's meant to be permanent.

Third: 'it's inside my boundary, so it's my business.' Planning control isn't about ownership — what you do on your own land is development or it isn't, wherever the red line runs. Fourth: 'building regs approval means the planning side's sorted.' Separate regimes doing separate jobs — building regulations are about the safety and construction of the building, planning about the use and development of land.

Fifth: 'it's been there for years, so it must be lawful.' Perhaps — but only if the time for enforcement has actually passed. The periods are specific and the evidence has to prove it; age alone confers nothing, the immunity rules do, with their own tests and timescales. And sixth: 'we dug a trench, so we've commenced.' Only if the works were lawful — in accordance with the permission and its pre-commencement conditions. Dig the trench in breach of a condition precedent and, on Whitley, you may have commenced nothing at all.

title: The sequence as a discipline
paras: So, back to the beginning, because the whole thing reduces to three questions in strict order — and the order is the method. Is it development? Apply the definition, remember the two limbs, check the exclusions. If it isn't, the system doesn't reach it and you can stop.

If it is, where does permission come from? Only two sources — the automatic grant of the Order, and an express grant on an application. Look to the Order first, and to an application only if the Order doesn't reach. And remember permitted development is a real permission, with real limits, real conditions, and that habitats trap inside it. Then, and only then, the third: has development lawfully begun? Discharge the pre-commencement conditions before you start, get the approvals in writing, record the works, and handle the levy before the first spade — because a permission that's never lawfully implemented is worth nothing at all.

None of this is difficult, and that's the point. The expensive mistakes in planning aren't made in the refinements; they're made at first principles — by the person who never asked whether it was development, who assumed the Order covered them, who dug a trench in breach of a condition and lost a permission worth a fortune. Get them right, in order, every time. One caveat to close: this is England only, general guidance rather than advice on any specific site, and always check the legislation as it stands today — the precise references are in the written guide.
